a b s t r a c t
The rapid development of automotive industry results in a series of increasingly serious
problems such as energy consumption and environmental pollution, so that developing
the automotive steels with high-strength and low-density is of great significance for energy
conservation and emission reduction. Recently, FeeMneCeAl system steel is favored by
numerous researchers because of its low density and excellent combination of strength
and ductility. However, too much Al addition inevitably triggers various changes of
microstructure, deformation mechanism, and mechanical properties. In this paper, the
composition design, production process, strengthening and strain hardening mechanism,
and microstructure evolution are systematically expounded. The discussion mainly fo-
cuses on various strengthening (solid solution strengthening, grain refinement strength-
ening and precipitation strengthening) and strain hardening mechanisms (phase
transformation-induced-plasticity (TRIP), twinning-induced-plasticity (TWIP), microband-
induced-plasticity (MBIP), shear-band-induced-plasticity (SIP) and dynamic slip band
refinement (DSBR), etc.). Also, the existing problems and future challenges in FeeMneAleC
low-density steels are pointed out via analyzing the service performance (cryogenic per-
formance, impact toughness, fatigue performance, hydrogen embrittlement, wear perfor-
mance, and tensile properties). Finally, we look forward to the future development
direction of FeeMneAleC low-density steels and provide the valuable ideas.

With the rapid development of automobile industry, fuel ef-
ficiency and greenhouse gas emissions become increasingly
serious. More and more advanced high-strength steel or
lightweight materials (such as magnesium alloy, aluminum
alloy, and carbon fiber materials) are employed in automobile
production towards the above issues via achieving light-
weighting. However, their expensive material cost and poor
service properties (formability, wear, and hydrogen
embrittlement et al.) result in a limited application in auto-

Low-density steels, which are considered as the new gen-
eration automobile materials, have been developed to over-
come the aforementioned shortages. As early as the 1930 s,
Korter and Ton [1] first put forward the concept of
FeeMneCeAl system steels with Ni and Cr additions in
consideration of the development prospect of high-strength
steels. To lower the cost and density together, Ham and
Carin [2] adopted the cheap Al and Mn elements instead of
expensive Ni and Cr elements to optimize the chemical
composition of stainless steels in the 1958 s. In the 1980 s and
1990 s [3e5], the replacement of Ni and Cr in stainless steel
was widely studied, whereas few scientific studies on low-
density steels were reported. Until the 2000 s, Frommeyer
et al. [6] systematically investigated the microstructure and
mechanical properties of FeeMneAleC low-density steels and
considered that this steel can be employed to equip automo-
bile steels. Since then, FeeMneAleC low-density steels star-
ted to attract much attention.
With the in-depth research of FeeMneCeAl steels in
recent years, it was found that Si addition presents a
competitive advantage, which could restrain the carbide pre-
cipitation and enhance the mechanical properties [7e12].
However, some other scholars insisted that the Si addition
played a negative role in improving the mechanical properties
of this steel [13,14]. It can be seen that the role of Si element in
FeeMneAleC steels is still controversial. In addition, Si
element is not the main chemical component in FeeMneAleC
low-density steels. Therefore, Si element will not be discussed
in the following sections.
In recent years, the research on low-density high-strength
steels mainly focuses on the composition design, role of
alloying elements, and microstructure characteristics. The
relationship between precipitates and matrix phases is also
widely studied by numerous researchers. In FeeMneAleC
steels, the variation of alloying element content results in the
changes of both microstructures and strain hardening
mechanisms, leading to the distant differences in application
performance [13e18]. Therefore, the present work will give a
brief introduction to alloying design and producing process.
Furthermore, this work summarizes various strengthening
and toughening mechanisms of single ferrite and austenite,
austenite base duplex phase (A-BDP), and ferrite base duplex
phase (F-BDP) steels with FeeMneAleC composition. Finally,
the existing problems and future challenges under different
service environments are investigated.

characteristics of FeeMneAleC low-density
steels
The composition design plays an important role in density
and microstructure characteristics, such as lattice constant,
phase composition and precipitate type. Thus, it is necessary
to summarize the composition design and role of alloying el-
ements, as well as the resulting influence on microstructure
characteristics of FeeMneCeAl low-density steels.

The room temperature microstructure of single ferrite
FeeMneAleC steels is d-ferrite. A high Al content results in an
increase of ferrite recrystallization temperature. So the d-
ferrite grain is hard to be refined due to the limited dynamic or
static recrystallizations [37]. Therefore, d-ferrite prolongs
along the rolling direction and presents the banded
morphology under hot rolling conditions. During the subse-
quent cooling process, k-carbide will precipitate along the d-
ferrite grain boundary if the cooling rate is slow. Moreover, Al
content can significantly influence the crystal structures of
matrix phases. Due to the difference in Al content, the disor-
dered FeAl phase with A2, ordered FeAl phase with B2, or or-
dered Fe Al phase with DO3 structures can act as the matrix
phases [38].
The room temperature microstructure of single austenite
FeeMneAleC steels is composed of equiaxed austenite
together with annealing twins [39], because the temperature
of thermal-mechanical processing is generally located within
the single austenite phase region. After cold rolling, the severe
plastic deformation makes numerous grains elongated into
lath-like morphology along the rolling direction. Due to the
differences in element contents and cooling rates, the carbide
types formed in austenite are k-carbide and B2/DO3. Gener-
ally, k-carbide can be divided into intragranular k0-carbides
and intergranular k<sup>*</sup>-carbides, as shown in Fig. 2 [40].
The microstructure of FeeMneAleC duplex phase low-
density steels is relatively complex, including austenite,
ferrite (a and d), B2, DO3, k-carbide, b-Mn, and other pre-
cipitates (Table 1). The substructure, size, volume fraction and
distributed location of these phases are different due to the
influence of ferrite and austenite recrystallization [37,41] and
element partitioning [18] under various heat-treatment pro-
cesses. The quenched microstructure of A-BDP steels is full
austenite. After aging at 500e800 C, the lath-like ferrite will

2.3. Other processes
To pursuit more outstanding combination between strength
and ductility, the scholars adopted some other thermal me-
chanical processing technologies. Ren et al. [54] adopted the
rapidly water-quenched to manufacture the short-range
ordering phase and k-carbide in a Fe-30.4Mne8Al-1.2C steel.
As the cooling rate increased, the transformation from short-
range ordering to k-carbide was restrained, which increased
the work hardening without deteriorating yield strength.
Kwang and Hyo et al. [55] developed a low-temperature
tempering-induced partitioning process to overcome the
strength-ductility trade-off in a Fe-2.8Mn-5.7Al-0.3C steel. The
austenite grains with heterogeneous size-distribution were
embedded in ferrite, which provided a suitable condition for C
partitioning. Interestingly, more C preferentially partitioned
into smaller austenite grains than larger ones. This size-
dependent partitioning led to the slip spacing variation and
lattice strain under dislocation motion.

and mechanical properties of FeeMneAleC low-density
steels. Table 2 summarizes the mechanical properties of

susceptible to annealing/aging temperatures and times. Thus,

optimize the existing process and to further narrow the tem-

(3) MC carbide strengthening
In recent years, the addition of micro-alloying element (Nb,
V and Ti et al.) has been widely employed to improve the
mechanical properties of FeeMneAleC low-density steels.
Due to a high affinity between micro-alloying (Nb, V and Ti
et al.) and C atoms, numerous stable MC carbides are formed,
effectively reducing the nucleation driving force of other car-
bides, thus inhibiting the precipitation and growth of other
carbides [57,58]. Song et al. [60] considered that the yield
strength increment from MC carbides was similar to that from
k-carbide in FeeMneAleC steels under suitable microstruc-
ture controlling. Zargaran et al. [59] confirmed that the 0.2 wt%
Nb addition into a Fee8Ale5Mn-0.1C steel could result in 0.2%
volume fraction of NbC precipitates, much lower than 2.3%
volume fraction of k-carbide. Although NbC precipitates have
poorer inhibition on k-carbide precipitation, the austenite
grain size is obviously refined. Compared with Nb-free steels
under the same conditions, the yield strength of Nb-
containing steel increases by about 100 MPa without deterio-
rating ductility. However, a few scholars hold different opin-
ions on the above conclusion. Li et al. [79] studied the effect of
Ti, Mo and Nb composite additions on microstructure and
tensile behavior of a Fe-26Mn-8Al–1.5C steel. It was found
that the additions of Ti, Mo and Nb could refine the grains,
increase the size and volume fraction of κ-carbide, and form
intercrystalline and intragranular (Ti, Mo, Nb)C particles. The
coarse k-carbide and nano (Ti, Mo, Nb)C particles on grain
boundary resulted in the poor ductility. It can be seen that
there is no agreed theory about the effect of MC carbide on κ-
carbide precipitation and growth, and further research is
needed.
Hereby, the Mn and C contents can affect the solution
strengthening, precipitation strengthening and austenite
characteristics. The rolling deformation and heat-treatment
technologies also influence the nucleation of various pre-
cipitates (k-carbide, B2, and MC), grain size and austenite
characteristics. However, the existing researches only focus
on a certain scientific problem, such as the role of recrystal-
lization annealing on MC precipitation behavior. The research
and development of FeeMneAleC low-density steel is still
under the gestation stage, and more systematic and in-depth
researches are needed in future.
3.2. Strain hardening mechanism
TRIP and TWIP effects are the main deformation mechanisms
for FeeMneAleC duplex phase low-density steels. When the
fractions of d-ferrite and austenite are high, the deformation
mechanisms show multi-stage strain hardening characteris-
tics. In addition, due to the absence of austenite in single
ferrite FeeMneAleC steels, martensite transformation is ab-
sent. For single austenite-base FeeMneAleC steels, the
deformation mechanism is closely related to stacking fault
energy (SFE).
3.2.1. Single ferrite steel
Al content strongly influences the tensile properties of single
ferrite-base FeeMneAleC steels by influencing crystal struc-
tures (Fig. 7) [80]. When the Al content reaches 6 wt%, the k
phase with a short-range ordering crystal structure is gradu-
ally formed, resulting in a sharp decrease of ductility [81].
With the increase of Al content over 7 wt%, the short-range
ordering reaction continuously occurs, and the shear action
of dislocations on ordered phases induces high work hard-
ening during plastic deformation [82]. Further increasing Al
content to a peak of 16 wt%, a terrific amount of B2 and DO3
phases with super crystal structures are formed, resulting in a
rapid decrease of work hardening [20]. Herrmann et al. [83]
observed dislocation slip bands in Fe-xAl steels, and they
believed that the generation and slip of dislocations in a
Fee6Al steel determined the deformation mechanism during
plastic deformation. As the Al content increased to 11e19 wt
%, the number of active mobile dislocations decreased under a
low deformation temperature, due to a limited number of
dislocation slip systems. At this time, the number of mobile
dislocations sensitively depended on crystal orientation. After
fracture, the dense dislocation bundles and undeformed B2
phase were also observed in ferrite, indicating that uneven
plastic deformation occurred in ferrite. The above discussion
implies that the shear of mobile dislocations on ordered
phases and dislocation slips mainly control the strain hard-
ening of single ferrite steels.

Frommeyer et al. [85] studied the tensile behavior of a

formed accompanied by dislocation slips. At the same time,
nano k-carbides were uniformly arranged on the austenitic
matrix with a certain spacing. In addition, the uniform shear
deformation (namely, the SIP effect) in austenite is very
beneficial to total elongation. The synergistic effect among
these deformation mechanisms results in the excellent me-
chanical properties.

20e30 wt%. After rolling, annealing and quenching treat-
ments, the microstructure consists of complete austenite
together with a large number of annealing twins. Hong et al.
[86] studied the formation mechanism of deformation twins
in a Fee17.5Mne1.5Al-0.85C TWIP steel (Fig. 8). They deemed

Shockley and Frank partial dislocations at positions slightly
away from the prior austenite grain boundary, finally forming
the stacking faults. Further straining to 0.05, deformation
twins formed near the austenite grain boundary and gradually
grew into the grains. Therefore, the strong dislocation move-

high strain hardening of TWIP steels.

high strain, the microbands gradually formed due to the
interaction between mobile dislocations and Taylor crystal
lattices. The total dislocation density continuously increased
with the increasing strain, leading to the high work hardening.

also refine grains and enhance the strength and toughness

partial areas. Under a low strain, dislocations aggregated on a
single slip plane and formed Taylor crystal lattices. Upon a
high strain, the microbands gradually formed due to the
interaction between mobile dislocations and Taylor crystal
lattices. The total dislocation density continuously increased
with the increasing strain, leading to the high work hardening.

also refine grains and enhance the strength and toughness

restrains the strain localization phenomenon in other sliding

4.4. Hydrogen embrittlement
Hydrogen embrittlement is the hydrogen dissolved in steels,
which causes stress concentration and then forms micro-
cracks, resulting in catastrophic fracture of the structural
material and component [112e115]. Once hydrogen embrit-
tlement is generated, it can not be eliminated. FeeMneAleC
low-density steels are considered as high-strength steels for
industrial applications. It is necessary to study the hydrogen
embrittlement sensitivity and its influence on mechanical
properties. Koyama et al. [112] insisted that the fracture
modes induced by hydrogen embrittlement were mainly
composed of intergranular and transgranular fractures in a
Fee18Mne1.2C steel. Meanwhile, the transgranular fracture
was initiated parallel to the primary and secondary defor-
mation twin boundaries, resulting in the generation of cracks
at grain boundaries and twin boundaries. Afterwards, they
examined the hydrogen-assisted cracking mechanisms of a
Fee26Mne11Ale1.2C steel [113]. They proposed that the grain
boundary triple junction cracking and slip-localization-
induced intergranular cracking along micro-voids deter-
mined the embrittlement ability. Meanwhile, grain boundary
triple junction cracking was preferentially generated on grain
boundaries, while the microscopically ductile slip-
localization-induced intergranular cracking assisted crack
growth during plastic deformation, resulting in the macro-
scopic brittle fracture appearance (Fig. 17).
In addition, the precipitates (k-carbide, B2, DO3, and b-Mn
et al.) also closely act with hydrogen and affect the hydrogen
embrittlement of FeeMneAleC steels [114]. Due to the high
SFEs, numerous k-carbides are often precipitated. Thus, the
hydrogen embrittlement is closely related to k-carbide parti-
cles [115]. It is reported that C content in FeeMneAleC steels
determined the hydrogen embrittlement [114]. For high C
(u > 1 wt%) steels, hydrogen embrittlement occurred in the
interdendritic area due to the presence of k-carbide, while the
k-carbide could limit crack propagation. For low C (u < 0.05 wt
%) steels, the hydrogen embrittlement occurred in DO3 phase.

resistance, and wear performance, it is widely used in auto-
mobile, military and construction fields. However, there are
still numerous scientific problems to be further studied. In
addition, basic research on the service properties of
FeeMneAleC low-density steels is insufficient. The investi-
gation of FeeMneAleC low-density steels can be started from
the following aspects.
(1) Alloy design. The variations of Mn, Al, and C contents
lead to the difference of phase constituents in
FeeMneAleC low-density steels and a wide range of
tensile properties can be acquired. Still, Al addition can
achieve the weight saving and microstructure
regulation, the limitation of Al addition should be
further adequately clarified to exploit its lightweight
role. The Mn, Al and C additions should be also tailored
properly to exert their advantage role in enhancing the
performance. In addition, the additions of micro-
alloying elements (Nb, V, Ti, Cr, and Ni et al.) need to
be explored so as to optimize the performance and
thereby broaden the service fields of FeeMneAleC low-
density steels.

nation between traditional hot/cold rolling and heat-
treatment to achieve comprehensive properties of
FeeMneAleC steels is feasible. However, the sensitivity
of properties to temperature and time easily results in a
series of problems in the industrial production lines. It
is necessary to explore and develop new processing
technologies. For instance, powder metallurgy could be
a promising method for manufacturing the
FeeMneAleC low-density steels.
(4) Strain hardening mechanism. The competition and
coupling among various strain hardening mechanisms
increase the difficulty for analyzing the deformation
behavior of FeeMneAleC steels. Moreover, the stress/
strain partitioning among various interfaces also
strongly affect microstructure evolution and deforma-
tion behavior. Simulation methods should be helpful for
analyzing the above-mentioned laws and problems.
(5) Service properties. Research work on the influence of
precipitation behavior on service properties of
FeeMneAleC low-density steels is still limited. Espe-
cially, the influence of short-range order and k-carbide
on service properties is still a debatable point. System-
atic research on the service properties of FeeMneAleC
lightweight steels is also needed.
In conclusion, the comprehensive properties of
FeeMneAleC low-density steels can be optimized by tailoring
the composition design, controlling the type, size and distri-
bution of various precipitates in the matrix, and optimizing
the technology parameters of thermal-mechanical processing
to meet the "strength, toughness, and lightweight" index and
further expand its application areas.
